name: Protein Structure Prediction
title: Protein Structure Prediction
answer: Protein structure prediction covers the computational task of taking an amino acid sequence and producing a three dimensional model of how that chain folds, including the positions of atoms and the contacts that hold the shape together. It sits inside drug discovery and molecular simulation because a reliable structure is often the starting point for understanding how a protein works, how a mutation changes it, and where a small molecule might bind. The field spans single chain prediction, multi chain complexes, and the modelling of how a protein moves between conformations. It is distinct from experimental structure determination by X-ray crystallography, cryo electron microscopy or nuclear magnetic resonance, though the two are used together.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Protein structure prediction covers the computational task of taking an amino acid sequence and producing a three dimensional model of how that chain folds, including the positions of atoms and the contacts that hold the shape together. It sits inside drug discovery and molecular simulation because a reliable structure is often the starting point for understanding how a protein works, how a mutation changes it, and where a small molecule might bind. The field spans single chain prediction, multi chain complexes, and the modelling of how a protein moves between conformations. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large neural networks trained on the Protein Data Bank, the public archive of experimentally solved structures, together with sequence databases and multiple sequence alignments that show how a protein family varies across species. Training and inference both need substantial GPU capacity, and the largest models are trained across many accelerators over days or weeks. Inference is lighter, and a single sequence can often be folded on one modern GPU in minutes, which is why web services and downloadable model weights have become common. Downstream work such as molecular dynamics or docking then runs on CPU clusters or GPU nodes with specialised simulation software.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pipeline starts with sequence retrieval and alignment, since evolutionary covariation between positions is a strong signal of which residues sit close in space. A model then predicts distances, angles or atom coordinates, often through a structure module that iteratively refines a set of frames, and the output is scored with confidence estimates per residue and per pair. Predicted structures are checked against known geometry, compared with any experimental data available, and frequently relaxed or refined before use. For drug discovery the structure is then used in binding site analysis, virtual screening or simulation, and predictions are treated as hypotheses to be tested rather than settled facts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because a predicted model is only as good as the sequence, the alignment and the model version that produced it, so labs are expected to record inputs, weights, parameters and confidence scores alongside the output. Licensing of model weights and of training data varies, and some structures carry restrictions from their source databases, which affects whether a model can be used commercially. In a medical or pharmaceutical setting, predicted structures that inform a development programme may fall under quality and documentation expectations similar to other computational evidence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward complexes rather than single chains, including protein assemblies, protein nucleic acid systems and interactions with ligands, and toward models that produce ensembles rather than one static shape. Integration with experimental data is deepening, so predictions are used to interpret cryo electron microscopy maps or to guide construct design. There is also growing interest in designing new proteins and binders rather than only predicting existing ones, which pulls the field closer to therapeutic development. As these models reach further into drug programmes, the open questions are less about raw accuracy and more about validation, reproducibility and how a prediction is weighed against experimental evidence.
